reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Defined by recurrent, stereotyped episodes of intense vomiting that are self-limiting and separated by well intervals of completely normal health
Attacks are strikingly similar for a given patient in onset time, duration, and symptom pattern, often starting in the early morning
Strong personal or family history of migraine is common, and the disorder is regarded as part of the migraine spectrum
Episodes may be triggered by psychological or physical stress, excitement, infection, sleep deprivation, or fasting
Prolonged hot bathing or showering to relieve symptoms should prompt consideration of coexisting cannabinoid hyperemesis
Management is split into prophylaxis between attacks (prophylactic anti-migraine agents) and abortive/supportive care during episodes with antiemetics, rehydration, and a calm dark environment
Diagnosis is largely clinical and requires exclusion of metabolic, neurological, and obstructive mimics
Coalescence of attacks or loss of symptom-free intervals suggests an alternative diagnosis or transformation
reference.pathophysiology: Cyclic vomiting syndrome is a functional gut-brain disorder in which recurrent, discrete episodes of severe nausea and vomiting arise on a background of normal health between attacks. The mechanism is thought to overlap with migraine, involving dysregulation of the brain-gut axis, autonomic instability, and heightened activation of central emetic pathways, with possible roles for mitochondrial energy dysfunction, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal stress responses, and altered neuroendocrine signalling. Triggers such as stress, infection, and fasting appear to lower the threshold for a stereotyped emetic cascade that then runs a self-limiting course.
additionalDifferentials: Intestinal malrotation with intermittent volvulus or other partial obstruction
Inborn errors of metabolism (e.g. urea cycle or fatty-acid oxidation defects)
Raised intracranial pressure or posterior fossa lesion
Adrenal insufficiency and other endocrine causes
Chronic nausea and vomiting syndrome or gastroparesis
additionalInvestigations: Basic metabolic panel, glucose, and assessment of hydration and acid-base status during an attack
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study or cross-sectional imaging to exclude malrotation and obstruction
Neuroimaging when neurological signs or atypical features are present
Metabolic screen (ammonia, lactate, organic acids) especially in younger or atypical patients
Upper endoscopy to exclude mucosal or structural upper-gut disease
Gastric emptying study when a motility disorder is suspected
redFlags: Bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, or signs of mechanical obstruction
Focal neurological deficit, severe headache, or vomiting worse on waking with papilloedema
Onset associated with fasting, intercurrent illness, or lethargy suggesting a metabolic crisis
Progressive weight loss or loss of the characteristic symptom-free intervals
reference.prognosis: Many children improve or remit with maturity, although a proportion evolve into migraine headaches, and adult-onset disease tends to be more chronic. With effective prophylaxis and trigger avoidance, attack frequency and severity can often be substantially reduced.
pitfalls: Attributing repeated presentations to a psychiatric or behavioural cause and missing the stereotyped pattern
Overlooking cannabinoid hyperemesis in patients who compulsively hot-bathe for relief
Failing to exclude malrotation or a metabolic disorder before labelling the illness functional
Under-treating dehydration and electrolyte loss during severe attacks
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Rome Foundation diagnostic criteria for functional gastrointestinal disorders
